title: Add 1 to a very big number
hook: Rounding errors hide in far decimal places. Surely whole numbers are safe?

knows: that 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 on a computer (pennies-dont-add-up)
doesNotKnow: that big numbers lose whole integers, not just tiny fractions
that a JavaScript number has 53 bits of precision

misconception: Rounding errors only hide in far decimal places; whole numbers are always safe.
objective: The learner can explain that a JavaScript number (a double) holds every whole number only up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992; just beyond it (up to 2^54) only every second whole number exists, so 9007199254740992 + 1 is rounded back to 9007199254740992 while + 2 works.

claims.text: In JavaScript, 9007199254740992 + 1 comes out as 9007199254740992, with no error or warning.
claims.source: Builder ran in Node 22: 2**53 + 1 === 2**53 is true. The stage computes the sums with real JavaScript arithmetic (Demo.tsx add()), and option B is the string of P + 1.

claims.text: A JavaScript number has room for only 53 binary digits (bits) of detail (a double, IEEE 754 binary64), and 2^53 is 2 multiplied by itself 53 times.
claims.source: ECMAScript 2024 Language Specification, 6.1.6.1 The Number Type (IEEE 754-2019 binary64); IEEE 754 binary64 has a 53-bit significand (52 stored + 1 implicit).

claims.text: Every whole number up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992 fits exactly, but just beyond it only every second whole number can be stored.
claims.source: ECMAScript 2024, 21.1.2.6 Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1); spacing of binary64 values in [2^53, 2^54) is 2. Builder checked: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER === 2**53 - 1; the stage's dots come from a BigInt round trip (Demo.tsx exact()). | Builder fix 2026-10-13 (pass 4): reworded to 'just beyond it (up to 2^54)' per fact-check; spacing is 2 on [2^53, 2^54), 4 on [2^54, 2^55).

claims.text: Past 2^53, adding 1 lands halfway between two storable numbers and is rounded to one of them, so it either does nothing or jumps by 2; adding 2 moves 9007199254740992 to 9007199254740994.
claims.source: Round-half-to-even is IEEE 754's default rounding (roundTiesToEven, 4.3.1). Builder ran in Node: 2**53 + 2 = 9007199254740994; (2**53 + 2) + 1 = 9007199254740996; (2**53 + 4) + 1 = 9007199254740996.

claims.text: For exact big whole numbers, JavaScript programmers use BigInt.

recall.question: A JavaScript program stores order IDs as ordinary numbers. Around 9,007,199,254,740,993 two different IDs start comparing as equal. Why?
options: The IDs overflowed and became negative
Past 2^53 a JavaScript number cannot hold every whole number, so neighbours round to the same value
recall.why: A double has 53 bits of precision, so just beyond 2^53 (up to 2^54) only every second whole number exists and an odd ID is rounded onto its neighbour.
